sections.title: CS and AI developments
sections.content:
Some “visual tool use” gains may come from the call scaffold, not the returned pixels

A new paper tests an unusually useful ablation for tool-augmented VLMs. Systems that “think with images” often emit a crop/zoom/code call, receive a new image, then continue reasoning. TextCall preserves the tool name, coordinates, target description and intent but replaces the returned image with [Image output skipped].

Across the authors’ LoRA, full-fine-tuning and RL settings, TextCall matches or exceeds the full image-return pipeline on the studied benchmark distributions. On matched training queries, scaffold-only input reaches equivalent accuracy, while latency falls 29–46% and external tool-execution calls disappear. Decomposing the scaffold suggests both natural-language reasoning and spatial code contribute.

The useful conclusion is not “pixels do not matter.” The authors explicitly limit the claim to current thinking-with-images benchmarks. If deleting the tool output preserves the score, a benchmark may be rewarding a serialized plan or location prior rather than evidence obtained from the new pixels. For a real perception system, this is exactly the ablation to run before paying runtime and engineering cost for an image tool. Paper

A video world model that numerically integrates motion instead of relearning every transition

Latent Dynamics Reasoning (LDR) represents motion in a structured latent, numerically integrates the lower-order kinematics, and trains the learned component mainly on the third- and higher-order residual needed to correct the rollout.

On the controlled PhyWorld suite—uniform motion, parabolas, collision, bouncing and looming—the paper reports an in-distribution/out-of-distribution error gap more than 20× smaller than its video-diffusion baseline, with 26× fewer parameters and 143× faster inference at 256². One severe-shift example trains only on red balls moving left-to-right and successfully predicts a blue square moving right-to-left.

This is a synthetic white-box physics benchmark, not proof for messy real-world video. The architectural bet is still useful: when part of the transition law is known and cheap, hard-code the integrator and spend learned capacity on the residual, instead of forcing a network to rediscover elementary dynamics from pixels. Paper

sections.title: Technical idea: the alias method makes weighted sampling constant-time
sections.content:
Suppose you repeatedly need to sample one item from a fixed categorical distribution. A cumulative-probability array plus binary search costs O(log n) per draw. The alias method pays an up-front table-building cost so each later sample takes constant time.

Scale the n probabilities so their mean is 1. Pair an underfull bucket with an overfull one: fill the leftover fraction of the underfull bucket with an alias pointing to the overfull item, then continue until every bucket has total mass 1. Each entry needs only a threshold and, when necessary, an alias index.

A draw becomes: choose a uniform bucket, generate one uniform number in [0,1), and return either the primary item or its alias. This is useful in rendering, Monte Carlo simulation and randomized load generation. The catch is mutability: frequently changing weights can require substantial rebuilding, so the method is strongest when the distribution is comparatively static and draws are numerous. Open-access overview

sections.title: Non-CS science: France’s heatwave creates a two-sided electricity squeeze
sections.content:
Today’s French power-price jump is a compact thermodynamics lesson. Day-ahead electricity rose about 20.5% to €141/MWh as the heatwave both raised cooling demand and tightened power supply. Forecast consumption for Wednesday was up by about 1.6 GW, with the national average temperature expected around 28.8°C, 7.4°C above normal.

A reactor’s fission heat ultimately becomes steam, drives a turbine, and then the remaining waste heat must be rejected through a condenser and cooling system. When the river or estuary used as the heat sink is already hot, plants have less thermal headroom. French sites also operate under environmental limits on how much their discharges may warm the receiving water. EDF explicitly reduces output at sites such as Blayais when Gironde temperatures require it, to protect aquatic ecosystems.

So the grid gets squeezed from both sides: air conditioning pushes demand upward while hot cooling water can constrain generation. Cooling towers reduce the river-temperature problem by rejecting more heat to the atmosphere but do not eliminate water and heat constraints. EDF says climate-related high-temperature/low-flow losses have averaged only about 0.3% of annual French nuclear production since 2000; the issue is less annual energy than short periods when several constraints coincide. Reuters · EDF on Blayais thermal limits · EDF on cooling systems

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• China’s latest Pacific missile test has exposed a regional security split. Reuters reports that July’s nuclear-capable ballistic-missile test into the Pacific—China’s first known such test there since September 2024—came hours after Fiji and Australia signed Fiji’s first defence alliance. Pacific foreign ministers then failed to agree on a collective condemnation. Small states gain surveillance, disaster-response, policing and training capacity from outside partnerships, while proliferating Chinese, U.S. and allied military arrangements make the region harder to keep outside great-power competition. Reuters
  • Colombia’s new government is pairing a security turn with fiscal austerity and hydrocarbon expansion. President Abelardo De La Espriella has pledged to freeze public spending, simplify taxes while retaining popular social programmes, expand oil and gas exploration including fracking, and intensify action against armed groups. A large fiscal deficit, public debt and political constraints limit how much tax cutting, social-program continuity and new security spending can coexist. Reuters
  • Russia’s overnight Ukraine strikes again targeted logistics and industrial capacity as well as cities. Moscow says it hit transport/logistics centres in Kyiv and the Zaporizhstal steel works in Zaporizhzhia because of their military role; Ukrainian officials reported six killed and 20 injured in Zaporizhzhia and fires in Kyiv. Warehouses, parcel/logistics hubs and steel production are dual-use infrastructure, so a long war increasingly attacks systems that move components and manufacture protective structures rather than only front-line formations. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment: Bukharin on making “imperialism” historically specific
sections.content:
“Imperialism is a policy of conquest. But not every policy of conquest is imperialism.”

— Nikolai Bukharin, Imperialism and World Economy, Chapter IX, “Imperialism as an Historic Category.” Primary text

Bukharin is arguing against a definition so broad that Alexander, Rome, Napoleon and modern capitalist states all become the same timeless phenomenon. For him, the form—conquest—is insufficient. The analytical question is which production relations and class structure the policy reproduces and expands. His answer for the early twentieth century is finance capital: banking and industrial capital fused into large national economic blocs competing within an already developed world economy.

The distinction remains useful even if you reject parts of his theory. Calling every expansionist state “imperialist” can identify a family resemblance but risks erasing what changes when the economic base, firms, state capacity and world market change. Bukharin’s own definition is correspondingly narrow and period-bound; that is a substantive thesis, not a neutral dictionary meaning.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Machiavelli: class conflict can produce liberty rather than merely threaten it

“it is in this conflict that all laws favourable to freedom have their origin”

— Niccolò Machiavelli, Discourses on Livy, Book I, Chapter 4, Ninian Hill Thomson translation. Primary text

Machiavelli defends the Roman conflicts between nobles and plebs against writers who see only disorder. Because elites want to dominate and ordinary citizens mainly want not to be dominated, conflict can force offices and laws that protect liberty. The claim is not that every riot is good; it is that political order can become freer by giving durable institutional expression to real social antagonisms.

Madison: faction is permanent, so politics becomes an architecture problem

“The latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man”

— James Madison, Federalist No. 10, 22 November 1787. Founders Online

Madison argues that destroying faction would require destroying liberty or homogenising interests. The constitutional problem is therefore to control faction’s effects through scale, representation and competing interests. Machiavelli asks how conflict can generate protections against domination; Madison asks how plural conflict can be prevented from turning into domination by a faction. Neither expects a healthy polity to abolish antagonism.

sections.title: French usage: mine de rien
sections.content:
Mine de rien is familiar French for doing, saying or noticing something without making a show of it / as if it were nothing. CNRTL glosses the adverbial expression as sans en avoir l’air.

  • Mine de rien, ça prend deux heures. — It doesn’t look like much, but it takes two hours / actually, it takes two hours.
  • Il a beaucoup avancé, mine de rien. — He’s quietly made a lot of progress.
  • Elle a posé la question mine de rien. — She asked the question casually, as though it were nothing.

The English rendering depends on context: quietly, casually, without making a fuss, actually, when you think about it can all work. Related but different: faire mine de + infinitive means to make as if / appear to do something: Il a fait mine de partir = “He made as if to leave.” CNRTL

sections.content: Three direct recommendations. Open the three-video YouTube queue.

items.label: Classical
items.piece: Shostakovich — Five Pieces for Two Cellos and Piano: Prelude
items.performer: Jeein You, Gautier Capuçon & Samuel Parent
items.description: 2:42. A deliberately short chamber pick after the recent large-form run: two cellos give the line a warm, vocal weight, while the piano keeps the little piece moving instead of letting it become a static miniature. The point is melodic immediacy and a complete arc in under three minutes, not short music as a new default.

items.label: Jazz / fusion
items.description: 4:02. Compact, keyboard-led contemporary fusion from Unity (2024), with a clear theme and polished ensemble writing. This tests a cleaner, more arranged lane adjacent to the Yellowjackets result rather than another spacious piano trio. The risk is that it lands too smooth/background-ish; if it does, that is useful information about where the line between coherent and overly polished sits.

items.label: Other
items.performer: Live on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert
items.description: 3:27. A stripped solo protest-folk performance built around guitar, vocal phrasing and blunt topical songwriting. Musically, this tests whether a concise, lyric-forward folk song can hold attention without dense arrangement or instrumental novelty; it also moves the third lane away from the recent instrumental-guitar, psych and French-pop sequence.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: a medieval receipt could be one stick split into two
sections.content:
For centuries, the English Exchequer used wooden tally sticks to record payments. Amounts were encoded as notches on a stick, and the stick was then split lengthwise. One half went to the collector or payer and the matching half remained with the Exchequer.

Because the two pieces came from the same irregular grain and carried the same notches before splitting, bringing the halves back together could authenticate the record without a shared database, signature algorithm or widespread literacy. It is a physical ancestor of the general idea behind a matched token: verification depends on two pieces derived from one original object.

The National Archives notes that many surviving Exchequer tallies were destroyed in the 1834 fire. The National Archives glossary

sections.title: Puzzle / dilemma: Parfit’s depletion case and the nonidentity problem
sections.content:
A society can choose between two long-term resource policies:

  • Conservation: people over the next two centuries are slightly worse off, but people in the distant future have a much higher quality of life.
  • Depletion: the next two centuries are slightly better, but distant-future quality of life is much lower—still worth living, but clearly worse than under conservation.

Now add the identity problem: choosing conservation rather than depletion changes economic conditions, migration, relationships and the timing of conceptions. After a few generations, the people who exist are almost certainly different people.

So a distant-future person under depletion cannot straightforwardly say, “You made me worse off than I would have been under conservation.” Under conservation, that person probably never exists at all; someone else does. If their life is still worth living, depletion may have harmed no future individual relative to that individual’s alternative.

Question: if a policy predictably creates a much worse future but makes no particular future person worse off than they otherwise would have been, what exactly makes the policy wrong? Do moral reasons have to be person-affecting, or can “this future is worse” be enough even when the identities differ? Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
